title: 01. Fundamentals & Trade-offs: Reliability
summary: Reliability is the probability that a system performs its intended function correctly under stated operating conditions for a specified period of time, encompassing correctness, fault tolerance, and continuity of service.
objectives: What is the difference between reliability and availability, and why does it matter for SLOs?
Explain MTBF and MTTR. How does each contribute to availability?
Compare active-active and active-passive redundancy. When would you choose each?
What is graceful degradation, and how does Netflix apply it to video playback?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Reliability is the probability that a system performs its intended function correctly under stated operating conditions for a specified period of time, encompassing correctness, fault tolerance, and continuity of service.

Reliability is one of the most misused words in system design because it is often conflated with availability. Availability answers "was the system up when a user reached for it?" — a binary up/down metric. Reliability is broader and stricter: it asks "did the system do the right thing, end to end, every single time, under the conditions we promised, for the duration we promised?" A system can be highly available but unreliable: imagine a payment gateway that responds to every request within 50ms but silently double-charges 0.1% of transactions. Its uptime is 100%, but its reliability is unacceptable because it is producing wrong outcomes. Conversely, a system can be reliable when it is up but unavailable if it goes offline frequently. In practice, reliability is the umbrella term and availability is one measurable component of it.

The classic formal model comes from hardware engineering: reliability `R(t) = e^(-λt)` for a constant failure rate λ, where λ is failures per unit time. Two operational metrics dominate the discussion. MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) is the average time the system runs correctly before failing. MTTR (Mean Time To Recovery) is the average time it takes to restore service after a failure. Availability itself can be derived from these: `A = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)`. To improve availability you either raise MTBF (fail less often) or lower MTTR (recover faster). Modern distributed systems target MTTR reduction aggressively — Netflix's Chaos Monkey intentionally kills production instances to force engineers to build systems that recover in seconds rather than hours. The cultural shift from "prevent all failures" to "embrace and recover from failures fast" is one of the defining moves of cloud-native engineering.

Why reliability matters in real systems comes down to trust and money. Amazon's checkout system is the canonical example: it must never go down, even on Prime Day when traffic spikes 3-5x and infrastructure is most stressed. Amazon has publicly stated that a 100ms increase in latency costs them 1% of sales; a checkout outage during a peak hour can cost tens of millions of dollars in a single hour, plus reputational damage that compounds over years. Netflix, serving 250+ million subscribers, runs Chaos Engineering in production (the Simian Army: Chaos Monkey, Latency Monkey, Conformity Monkey, Security Monkey, Doctor Monkey) precisely because they need empirical evidence that their system is reliable under partial failure, not theoretical confidence from pre-prod testing. A reliable system is one that has been observed to survive realistic failure scenarios, not one that has been merely designed to.

Redundancy is the primary mechanism for raising MTBF and lowering MTTR. There are two main redundancy patterns. In active-active deployment, multiple replicas serve traffic simultaneously; if one fails, the others absorb the load with no visible disruption but the system must handle split-brain and consistency. In active-passive, one replica serves while others stand by; failover is slower (typically seconds to minutes) but operationally simpler and cheaper. Active-active is preferred for stateless, read-heavy workloads (CDN edge nodes, API frontends); active-passive is common for stateful systems where consistency is paramount (primary-replica databases like PostgreSQL streaming replication, or Redis Sentinel-managed failover). The trade-off: active-active gives better MTTR but requires consensus and conflict resolution; active-passive is simpler but has a measurable failover gap.

Graceful degradation is the second pillar of reliability. A perfectly reliable system never has to degrade, but no real system achieves that — so the question becomes what happens when a dependency fails. A reliable system sheds optional functionality and continues serving the critical path. Netflix's playback service, for example, will continue serving video even if the personalized recommendation service is down — it falls back to a cached "trending now" list. Amazon's product page degrades to a simpler layout if the reviews service times out, but the Add to Cart button keeps working. This requires that engineers explicitly rank features by criticality at design time, build fallback paths, and test them. The pitfall is silent coupling: services that look independent in a diagram often share a downstream dependency (the same database, the same identity provider, the same CDN config), and when that shared dependency fails, every "graceful" fallback breaks at once. Reliability engineering therefore demands dependency mapping and blast-radius analysis, not just per-service resilience patterns.

Reliability connects to almost every other system design concept. It is constrained by availability (you cannot be reliable if you are down), it depends on durability (data must survive crashes for the system to behave correctly), it requires fault tolerance (the system must continue operating through partial failures), and it interacts with latency (a system that is up but takes 30 seconds to respond is not reliable from the user's perspective). Reliability is also in tension with cost: each additional nine of reliability typically costs an order of magnitude more in infrastructure, redundancy, and operational maturity. Senior engineers know that 100% reliability is not a goal — it is a trap — and instead target the right reliability level for each workload, with explicit error budgets that quantify how much unreliability the business can absorb.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Service Request] --> B{Healthy?} B -- Yes --> C[Process Correctly] C --> D[Record Success
MTBF timer runs] B -- No --> E[Failure Detected] E --> F[Trigger Failover] F --> G{Active-Active?} G -- Yes --> H[Redirect to Healthy Replica
MTTR: ~seconds] G -- No --> I[Promote Passive Replica
MTTR: ~minutes] H --> J[Restore Service] I --> J J --> K[Update MTTR Metric] D --> L["Compute Availability
A = MTBF/(MTBF+MTTR)"] K --> L ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-----------------+ +-----------------+ | Replica A | | Replica B | | (active) | | (active) | +--------+--------+ +--------+--------+ | | +------- shared -----------+ | load balancer | | | +------v------+ +-----v-------+ | Client | | Client | | requests | | requests | +-------------+ +-------------+ Failure on Replica A: +------!------+ | X down | +-------------+ +-------------+ | Replica B | | | absorbs all | +---- failover ----->| traffic | +-------------+ MTTR = detection time + failover time MTBF = uptime between failures ``` ### Walkthrough 1. A request arrives at the load balancer and is routed to a healthy replica. As long as the replica processes the request correctly, the MTBF timer continues to accumulate uptime. 2. A failure occurs (process crash, network partition, hardware fault). The health check or heartbeat detects it within the detection window — typically 3–10 seconds depending on the configured timeout. 3. The load balancer stops sending traffic to the failed replica. In active-active mode, surviving replicas absorb the load immediately; in active-passive mode, the standby is promoted, which adds promotion time to MTTR. 4. The failed replica is restarted, re-joined to the cluster, and verified healthy. MTTR ends when service is fully restored. 5. Availability is recomputed as `MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)` over the rolling window, feeding into SLO dashboards and error budgets.

sections.title: Code

quiz.question: What is the difference between reliability and availability, and why does it matter for SLOs?
options: An error budget is the inverse of an SLO: if your SLO is 99.9% availability, you have a 0.1% error budget per measurement window — about 43 minutes of downtime per month.
Chaos engineering is the discipline of running controlled failure experiments in production to validate that the system actually degrades gracefully when components fail.
Graceful degradation is the design pattern where a system, on losing a non-critical dependency, continues serving the critical path with reduced functionality rather than failing entirely.
Availability is the fraction of time the system is up: A = uptime / (uptime + downtime).
quiz.explanation: Availability is the fraction of time the system is up: A = uptime / (uptime + downtime). Reliability is broader — it asks whether the system produced correct results under the conditions promised, for the entire duration. A payment gateway that is up 100% but silently drops 0.1% of transactions is available but not reliable.

quiz.question: Explain MTBF and MTTR. How does each contribute to availability?
options: The Skip Intro button is on the critical playback path; the recommendation service is not.
The checkout service is Amazon's most reliability-critical path — it must not go down, and it must not silently drop or double-charge orders.
Current availability is 200 / (200 + 0.5) = 99.75%, which is two nines.
MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) is the average uptime between two consecutive failures.
quiz.explanation: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) is the average uptime between two consecutive failures. MTTR (Mean Time To Recovery) is the average time to restore service after a failure. Availability is A = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).

quiz.question: Compare active-active and active-passive redundancy. When would you choose each?
options: Availability of 99.9% measures only whether the service was up; it does not capture whether notifications were delivered within the user-expected SLA.
The Skip Intro button is on the critical playback path; the recommendation service is not.
The checkout service is Amazon's most reliability-critical path — it must not go down, and it must not silently drop or double-charge orders.
Active-active runs multiple replicas serving live traffic simultaneously; if one fails, others continue with no visible gap.
quiz.explanation: Active-active runs multiple replicas serving live traffic simultaneously; if one fails, others continue with no visible gap. It gives the lowest MTTR (effectively zero, since surviving replicas already serve) and the highest throughput because all capacity is utilized.

quiz.explanation: Graceful degradation is the design pattern where a system, on losing a non-critical dependency, continues serving the critical path with reduced functionality rather than failing entirely. Netflix's playback page has many subsystems: personalized recommendations, artwork personalization, subtitles, chapter markers, ratings, preview trailers. None of these are required to actually start playing the video.

quiz.explanation: An error budget is the inverse of an SLO: if your SLO is 99.9% availability, you have a 0.1% error budget per measurement window — about 43 minutes of downtime per month. As long as you stay under that budget, you are allowed to take risks (deploy new code, push features, run experiments). When the budget is exhausted, all further changes are frozen until the budget regenerates or the window resets.
